# Implications of the FDA’s new plausible mechanism framework for the development of a personalized in vivo prime editing platform

**Authors:** Emily R. Feierman; Madelynn N. Whittaker; Aidan Quigley; Dominique L. Brooks; Paige McVeigh; Angela X. Nan; Alvin Hsu; Hooda Said; Ousamah Younoss Soliman; Ryan Giovenco; Beverly L. Davidson; Mohamad-Gabriel Alameh; David R. Liu; Xiao Wang; Kiran Musunuru; Rebecca C. Ahrens-Nicklas

## Abstract

In February 2026, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) published a draft guidance on a new plausible mechanism framework for the development and approval of individualized therapies for genetic conditions. Here, we report initial proof-of-concept studies supporting a customizable prime editing platform geared to the treatment of 7 urea cycle disorders (UCDs) and other liver-centered disorders, as well as the outcome of a formal meeting with the FDA to discuss the use of the platform in an “umbrella-of-umbrellas” clinical trial including subjects with any of the 7 UCDs. We anticipate our findings will be of interest to academic investigators and industry sponsors who wish to pursue expeditious FDA approvals of therapies for ultra-rare diseases using the plausible mechanism framework.

## Abstract

The authors report initial proof-of-concept studies supporting a customizable prime editing platform geared to the treatment of 7 urea cycle disorders and other liver-centered disorders, as well as the outcome of a formal meeting with the FDA to discuss an “umbrella-of-umbrellas” clinical trial under the new plausible mechanism framework.

## Introduction

We have previously reported the development of an individualized base editing therapy, administered to an infant with neonatal-onset carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 (CPS1) deficiency (MIM: 237300), a type of urea cycle disorder (UCD), under a single-patient expanded-access investigational new drug (IND) application to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA).1 Following this, we outlined a potential path to the development of customizable in vivo base editing platforms for 7 infantile-onset UCDs and for phenylketonuria (PKU [MIM: 261600]) defined through formal interactions with the FDA.2 The FDA subsequently announced a “plausible mechanism framework” for the rapid development and approval of individualized therapies3 and on February 23, 2026, published a draft guidance outlining the new framework.4 The framework is highly consistent with the feedback we received via our interactions with the FDA,2 and the UCDs seem well suited to requirements of the framework: (1) “identifying a specific genetic, cellular, or molecular abnormality with a clear connection between specific alteration and disease indication” (typically achieved via gene panel testing, exome sequencing, or whole-genome sequencing in patients with a UCD); (2) “developing a therapy that targets the underlying or proximate pathogenic biological alterations” (which can be achieved with corrective gene editing); (3) “relying on a well-characterized natural history of the disease in an untreated population” (which is generally true for the UCDs as a group and particularly true for the more frequent individual UCDs); (4) “confirming that the target was successfully drugged or edited or both” (which can be documented with biochemical assessments related to the urea cycle); and (5) “demonstrating improvement in clinical outcomes or course.”4 To better understand how the framework might concretely apply to the treatment of UCDs, we proposed a personalized in vivo prime editing platform and requested feedback from the FDA via a Pre-IND meeting. In this perspective, we report the feedback from the FDA and our specific learnings.

## Proof of concept of a prime editing platform

Our previous efforts related to the treatment of UCDs, funded by the National Institutes of Health’s Somatic Cell Genome Editing (SCGE) program, have been facilitated by the ability to efficiently deliver base editors to the liver via a single drug product comprising lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) encapsulating a base editor mRNA and a single variant-specific guide RNA (gRNA). Base editing can address only a subset of patient variants, primarily those that can be corrected with an A>G or C>T change on the sense or antisense strand of a gene.5,6 To more comprehensively address genetic diseases with unmet medical needs, other editing approaches are needed. Prime editing is attractive due to its versatility, readily addressing all types of single-nucleotide variants and small insertion or deletion (indel) variants.7 A current limitation of prime editing is the difficulty of achieving efficient in vivo prime editing with a single LNP drug product, due to the need for multiple gRNAs (typically a prime editing gRNA [pegRNA] and a nicking gRNA [ngRNA]) and the pegRNA being much longer than a standard gRNA, making chemical synthesis at high purity a technically challenging task.

We therefore pursued a different prime editing strategy using two drug products: an LNP drug product encapsulating only a single mRNA encoding a prime editor protein and an adeno-associated viral (AAV) vector encoding the gRNAs.8 Advantages of this strategy include the following. (1) Because Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9 (SpCas9) gRNAs can each be expressed from a cassette of a few hundred base pairs, multiple gRNAs can be expressed from a single AAV vector; indeed, it is quite feasible to have multiple expressed copies of the same pegRNA/ngRNA or even distinct sets of pegRNAs/ngRNAs that allow for simultaneous correction of compound heterozygous variants in a patient. (2) The AAV vector expresses RNAs only, with no expressed protein, reducing immune responses. (3) Transient mRNA/LNP-mediated delivery of the prime editor further reduces immune responses and limits off-target editing. (4) Because the AAV vector constitutively expresses the gRNAs for a prolonged period (months to years), it is feasible to initiate additional rounds of prime editing with repeat dosing of the LNP drug product. (5) Although AAV serotype 8 (AAV8) and standard LNPs independently transduce multiple cell types in the liver,9,10 the overlap cell type that each delivery method preferentially transduces is the hepatocyte, the target cell type for treatment of UCDs.

We tested the AAV/LNP strategy with the ASS1 (argininosuccinate synthase 1; MIM: 603470) c.1168G>A (GenBank: NM_054012.4) (p.Gly390Arg) variant, which is one of the most frequently recurrent severe variants causing citrullinemia type 1 (MIM: 215700) and, indeed, causing any UCD.11 Analysis of the correlation between residual enzyme activity and severity of disease suggests that for patients with citrullinemia type 1, a threshold of 8.1% residual ASS enzymatic activity in the liver distinguishes severe disease from attenuated disease, indicative of a low therapeutic editing threshold.12 To expeditiously identify a prime editing solution for the ASS1 c.1168G>A (p.Gly390Arg) variant, we generated a lentivirus-transduced HuH-7 cell line harboring the variant, using a previously described methodology.1 (Multiple attempts to use prime editing to cleanly introduce the variant into the endogenous ASS1 locus in HuH-7 cells were unsuccessful.) Using the p.Gly390Arg lentivirus-transduced HuH-7 cell line, we screened the 50 top pegRNAs nominated by OptiPrime, a new machine learning model of prime editing efficiency,13 in combination with ngRNAs and the PE6c prime editor14 in plasmid transfection experiments using previously published methods15 (Figure 1A). In principle, these experiments could serve as the basis for potency assays for the clinical AAV and LNP drug products. Although lentivirus-transduced HuH-7 cell lines have limitations with respect to modeling in vivo editing efficiency (e.g., not assessing editing in the endogenous gene locus and using transformed cells that reflect a different cellular state from in vivo hepatocytes), the alternatives also have serious limitations. Induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived hepatocyte-like cells diverge from authentic hepatocytes in biologically important ways and suffer from immaturity and heterogeneity in the differentiation protocol.19,20 Neither iPSC-derived hepatocyte-like cells nor primary human hepatocytes are amenable to the development of master cell banks and working cell banks that can facilitate rigorous potency assays, in contrast to transformed or immortalized cell lines that are commonly used for that purpose.

To perform in vivo testing of the AAV/LNP strategy, we generated humanized mice with the ASS1 c.1168G>A (p.Gly390Arg) variant in the endogenous Ass1 locus via homologous recombination in mouse embryonic stem cells. Heterozygous mice (ASS1G390R/+) were healthy, whereas homozygous mice (ASS1G390R/ASS1G390R) survived no longer than 24 h after birth, consistent with past studies of Ass1-knockout mice.21 For this reason, we used only heterozygous knockin mice for studies of in vivo prime editing. We administered the AAV vector to mice approximately 6 weeks of age, followed by the LNPs 2 weeks later; we extracted whole-liver genomic DNA upon necropsy 1 week later. In initial small pilot studies, either the AAV dose was varied and the LNP dose was held constant or the LNP dose was varied and the AAV dose was held constant. Even at submaximal doses, the mean whole-liver corrective editing of the ASS1 c.1168G>A (p.Gly390Arg) variant in each dose group was as high as ≈30%–40% (Figures 2B–2D and 2F), well above the estimated editing threshold needed for clinical benefit for a patient with citrullinemia type 1 and homozygous for the ASS1 c.1168G>A (p.Gly390Arg) variant (≈5%–10%).12 Although the identity of the specific cell types in the liver in which the observed editing occurred remains to be established, the shared biodistribution of the AAV8 vector and LNPs to hepatocytes,9,10 as well as the predominant expression of ASS1 in hepatocytes among the liver cell types and thus increased accessibility of the ASS1 locus, argue for the editing preferentially occurring in hepatocytes. (All procedures used in our mouse studies were approved by the institutional animal care and use committees at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia and the University of Pennsylvania, where the studies were performed, and were consistent with local, state, and federal regulations, including the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals, as applicable.)

We acknowledge the limitations of this prime editing platform. The AAV vectors may persist in cells for years as episomes, continuing to express the gRNAs. In the absence of expression of a prime editor protein that can engage the gRNAs, there are unlikely to be any long-term deleterious consequences, although the potential for biological effects of any kind remains to be ruled out. There is the possibility of integration of AAV vectors into the genome, particularly when LNP-delivered prime editor protein is present in cells, as nicking of DNA (especially at the on-target site) may predispose to integration events. The prime editor would only be active in cells for a brief period of time, limiting the window when integration may occur. The absence of an RNA Pol II promoter in the AAV vector sequence makes it less likely that AAV integration would result in aberrant expression of a nearby gene.

Contamination with plasmid sequences and helper viruses has been reported in the human liver following AAV treatment,22 highlighting the need for stringent manufacturing procedures and analytical methods (which are an important aspect of the plausible mechanism framework, as described below). Although the same clinical LNP prime editor batch could be used for a number of patients, it is expected that an individualized AAV drug product will be needed for each patient, which paradoxically could present a challenge in downscaling clinical vector production to small-sized batches. Repeat LNP dosing could be confounded by immune responses to the prime editor protein, although repeat dosing of editing therapies has proven successful in patients,1,23 suggesting that even if immune responses occur, they do not impair LNP delivery and subsequent editing in target cells.

## Proposal for the deployment of a personalized prime editing platform in a clinical trial

With these preliminary proof-of-concept data in hand and mindful of the potential use of the new plausible mechanism framework to develop various applications of the prime editing platform for ultra-rare diseases, we requested a Pre-IND meeting with the FDA to discuss the use of the platform for the treatment of infantile-onset UCDs caused by variants in any of 7 genes—ASS1, CPS1 (MIM: 608307), OTC (MIM: 311250), ASL (MIM: 207900), ARG1 (MIM: 207800), NAGS (MIM: 237310), or SLC25A15 (MIM: 238970)—that encode enzymes or a transporter involved in the urea cycle. Each of these UCDs can manifest with hyperammonemic crises soon after birth, potentially resulting in permanent brain injury, coma, and death. Temporizing medical therapy entails the use of nitrogen scavenger medications and a protein-restricted diet. Liver transplantation, typically delayed for at least 9–12 months after birth in order to reduce surgical morbidity and mortality, is the definitive therapy and largely normalizes metabolism for each of these UCDs.24 In principle, liver-directed prime editing could sufficiently correct at least one pathogenic allele in the vast majority (>95%) of individuals affected by infantile-onset UCDs to ameliorate disease and relieve the need for transplantation.

We proposed a primary IND application with a master protocol for a phase 1/2 “umbrella-of-umbrellas” clinical trial,2 with the initial focus on the ASS1 c.1168G>A (p.Gly390Arg) variant. A single good laboratory practice (GLP)-like nonhuman primate biodistribution/toxicology study comprising 3 treatment groups would support the entire platform: (1) high-dose AAV treatment, followed 2 weeks later by high-dose LNP treatment, followed 6 h later by necropsy; (2) high-dose AAV treatment, followed 2 weeks later by high-dose LNP treatment, followed 2 weeks later by necropsy; and (3) high-dose AAV treatment, followed 2 weeks later by lower-dose LNP treatment, followed 4 weeks later by a repeat lower-dose LNP treatment, followed 13 weeks later by necropsy (this last treatment group being intended to support repeat LNP dosing in patients). New ASS1 variants would be added via amendment in real time to the primary IND with in vitro on-target editing and off-target editing data alone—i.e., there would be no need for additional animal studies—and upon approval, subjects with the added variants could be enrolled in the trial. For each of the other 6 UCD-associated genes, a secondary gene-specific IND application heavily cross-referencing the primary IND would be submitted, each starting with a representative gene variant, with new variants in the gene added via amendment in real time. The master protocol would be amended in concert with the addition of each new gene-specific IND application.

For each new variant, on-target editing solutions would be assessed and optimized in lentivirus-transduced HuH-7 cell lines, as performed for the ASS1 c.1168G>A (p.Gly390Arg) variant (Figure 1A). Potential sites of off-target editing would be nominated by nuclease-based techniques, with the premises that (1) prime editing requires an initial nicking event by the SpCas9 nickase portion of the prime editor and so the nomination of nick sites would identify all possible sites of prime editing and (2) the sites of nicks induced by a SpCas9 nickase with a gRNA would be essentially identical to the sites of double-strand breaks induced by the corresponding SpCas9 nuclease with the same gRNA. In keeping with past FDA guidance that at least two orthogonal off-target nomination methods should be used,25 with at least one method required to be an unbiased genome-wide assessment and one method permitted to be based on in silico prediction of potential off-target editing sites by homology to the gRNA target sequence, we would use the methods circularization for high-throughput analysis of nuclease genome-wide effects by sequencing (CHANGE-seq)26 and oligonucleotide enrichment and sequencing (ONE-seq),27 respectively. Candidate off-target sites would be verified in AAV/LNP-treated HuH-7 cells and primary human hepatocytes, at a minimum. There would also be a genome-wide assessment for AAV integration, using the integration site pipeline for paired-end reads (INSPIIRED).28

There would be as many as 7 distinct but interconnected INDs, one for each UCD-associated gene, with a single phase 1/2 clinical trial. The proposed major safety endpoint would be the incidence of treatment-emergent adverse events, and the proposed major efficacy endpoint would be the proportion of the study cohort who could tolerate an increase in protein intake to 100% of the FDA recommended dietary allowance for age (if not tolerating prior to treatment) and/or a substantial reduction in the nitrogen scavenger medication dose, without associated hyperammonemia, by 52 weeks after treatment. Proposed exploratory endpoints would include assessments of biomarkers such as plasma ammonia, plasma glutamine, and blood urea nitrogen (BUN). Although there are important differences in severity and clinical presentation among the UCDs—some of the UCDs are more likely to present with significant hyperammonemia and to present at a young age—the use of common inclusion criteria, such as a history of a plasma ammonia level exceeding a certain threshold level before a certain age, would account for these differences and identify individual patients with the same degree of unmet medical need regardless of the specific UCD.

Upon enrollment and treatment of 5 subjects spanning at least 3 UCDs, we could potentially have an end-of-phase 2 meeting with the FDA to determine what additional work would be needed for an accelerated approval or a full approval under the plausible mechanism framework (consistent with FDA feedback on our previous proposal for an LNP base editing platform for the treatment of UCDs2).

## Discussion of the prime editing platform with the FDA and the implications of the plausible mechanism framework

In our Pre-IND interaction, the FDA was generally supportive of the proposed prime editing platform (Figure 3). With respect to the nonclinical aspects of the work plan, the FDA felt that in vivo proof-of-concept studies were necessary to establish the biological activity of one version (“variant”) of the AAV and LNP drug products. Thus, they requested more comprehensive proof-of-concept studies with ASS1G390R/+ mice (acknowledging the impracticality of using perinatal lethal ASS1G390R/ASS1G390R mice), including defining the minimal effective AAV and LNP dose levels, evidence of hepatic delivery of the components of the prime editor (expression of the PE6c, pegRNA, and ngRNA transgenes), evidence of target engagement in the liver (corrective prime editing at the DNA level or increased ASS protein level), defining the time course of editing with multiple post-treatment necropsy time points, assessment of the effects of repeat dosing (i.e., increased prime editing), and analysis of biodistribution (PE6c, pegRNA, ngRNA, and on-target editing). (Although the FDA did not specifically request analysis of the overlap between AAV delivery and LNP delivery at cellular resolution in the mouse liver, such an analysis would be informative.) Importantly, the FDA agreed that for any additional variants beyond ASS1 c.1168G>A (p.Gly390Arg), no further animal studies would be necessary if the effective dose AAV and LNP dose levels could be modeled in vitro.Figure 3Conceptual overview of platform approach and regulatory strategy after discussion with the FDAGenes paired with diseases: ASS1, citrullinemia type 1; OTC, ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency; ASL, argininosuccinic acid (ASA) lyase deficiency; NAGS, N-acetylglutamate synthase (NAGS) deficiency; CPS1, carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 (CPS1) deficiency; ARG1, arginase deficiency; SLC25A15, hyperornithinemia-hyperammonemia-homocitrullinuria (HHH) syndrome. For the single nonhuman primate toxicology study, the FDA requested biodistribution analyses of both the AAV and LNP components, spanning the 3 necropsy time points. We agreed upon an adaptive study design in which an initial animal group would be tested with higher AAV and LNP doses initially, and if adverse effects were observed, an additional animal group would be tested with moderately lower AAV and LNP doses, and so forth, until no-observed-adverse-effect levels (NOAELs) were established, which would then inform clinical dosing. Finally, the FDA generally accepted the proposed off-target assessment strategy, with an emphasis on long-read sequencing to assess for AAV integration at the on-target site.

With respect to the clinical work plan, the FDA agreed that we could undertake a single umbrella-of-umbrellas phase 1/2 clinical trial with all 7 UCDs under a master protocol. (We note that the draft guidance for the plausible mechanism framework does not specify criteria for other disease groups that would qualify for this kind of umbrella-of-umbrellas trial.) The FDA confirmed that each UCD-associated gene would require its own IND application (primary IND with ASS1 and secondary gene-specific INDs) and, moreover, that each gene would require its own biologics license application (BLA) for marketing authorization, although much of the same data could be reused across the INDs and BLAs. Although the FDA did not feel that 5 subjects spanning at least 3 UCDs would be sufficient to support BLAs for all 7 UCD-associated genes, it signaled potential flexibility. Specifically, it may be possible to leverage data from the initial 5 subjects in each of the 7 BLAs, if combined with data from a limited number of additional subjects with each specific UCD to support each gene-specific BLA. These additional subjects could be treated in a phase 3 extension of the original trial. The BLAs could then be filed in a staggered fashion, depending on the recruitment pattern of subjects with different UCDs.

The FDA agreed with the general design of the master protocol for an open-label, single-arm study spanning all 7 UCDs. Although a randomized controlled study would not be required given the rarity of each UCD, the FDA nonetheless indicated that it would be important to choose a comparator that would be used for all comparative analyses for efficacy and safety, so that the master protocol would constitute an “adequate and well-controlled study” in accordance with 21 CFR § 314.126, which governs FDA approvals. We discussed the possibility of having each subject serve as their own control, which the FDA felt could be applicable to the UCDs “if the effect of [the] treatment is dramatic or self-evident, occurs rapidly following treatment, and is unlikely to have occurred spontaneously,” in accordance with the draft guidance.4 Data prospectively collected during the screening period for each subject (likely to span at least 1 month, due to the time needed to manufacture an individualized drug product) could serve as a comparator for data collected post-treatment. Finally, the FDA agreed that the proposed end-of-phase 2 meeting was the appropriate time to discuss the requirements for potential BLA submissions.

With respect to chemistry, manufacturing, and controls (CMCs), the FDA indicated that if data from subjects treated in the phase 1/2 clinical study were to be used to support BLAs, the CMC requirements would need to be much more stringent than would be typical for early-phase clinical trials. (1) Ideally, the manufacturing process and facility would be finalized before the phase 1/2 study was initiated to avoid the need for subsequent comparability studies if the process or facility were to be changed midway through the study. (2) Ideally, the process validation plan would be discussed and agreed upon with the FDA before the phase 1/2 study was initiated. (3) It would not be necessary to manufacture identical drug product lots for process performance qualification (PPQ), but rather, data from multiple individualized “variant” drug product lots could be used for PPQ if it could be demonstrated that the manufacturing process was consistent across the lots. (4) The individualized drug product lots made for the treatment of phase 1/2 subjects would need to be used for PPQ. (5) Enhanced in-process sampling and testing would be needed to support process validation and qualification for these phase 1/2 PPQ lots. (6) The manufacturing facility for these phase 1/2 PPQ lots would need to be fully current good manufacturing practice (cGMP) compliant and inspection ready before producing the lots. (7) Ideally, all analytical methods used to support product quality and process control would be fully validated before the phase 1/2 study was initiated. (8) Stability testing would need to be performed for all individualized drug product lots manufactured for the phase 1/2 study, using validated assays. (9) Although the proposed variant-specific cellular potency assays (similar in concept to the assays shown in Figure 2A) would be acceptable, they would nonetheless need to be validated across different individualized drug product variants in such a way as to permit new variants to be rigorously assessed.

The FDA indicated that there could be flexibility in these requirements for the early phase 1/2 subjects but that the requirements would need to be in place for the late phase 1/2 subjects. Another possibility would be to defer the requirements until a phase 3 extension, although that would likely lengthen the timeline and increase the number of subjects needed for BLA submissions. Notably, the draft guidance allows for the use of “prior knowledge” (manufacturing process and control strategies, process validation, and qualified analytical methods) from a closely related drug product. In other words, once a development program for a drug product for one disease set is sufficiently mature (e.g., UCDs), a subsequent program for essentially the same drug product (e.g., AAV or LNP for prime editing) for another disease set (e.g., organic acidemias) could be greatly streamlined by heavily relying on the validated manufacturing process, PPQ data, analytical assays, etc., from the first program.

## Conclusions

The draft guidance for the plausible mechanism framework creates an unprecedented opportunity for the development and approval of therapies for ultra-rare genetic diseases, particularly therapies that are individualized to patients. However, based on the language in the guidance (which remains to be finalized) and the FDA’s feedback on our proposed prime editing platform for UCDs, an abbreviated pathway to an FDA approval—entailing only a single clinical trial—appears to be dependent on a sponsor’s ability to apply the strict requirements ordinarily reserved for late-stage clinical trials to an early-stage clinical trial. In our judgment, companies already deeply engaged in mature gene editing development programs are best positioned to take advantage of the plausible mechanism framework for future programs. Given the way the draft guidance is currently written, academic investigators aspiring to develop individualized therapies for ultra-rare diseases all the way up to FDA approval—a likely prerequisite for the payer reimbursements needed to make broad deployment of the therapies economically viable—would be best served to work very closely with those companies in order to succeed in their mission. In that light, we encourage our colleagues to consider alternative ways in which the framework could be creatively engaged to serve rare disease populations and to provide feedback to the FDA while the public comment period for the draft guidance remains open.

It should be noted that, as always, Pre-IND feedback from the FDA is non-binding and subject to change. That notwithstanding, in the expectation that they would be useful to academic investigators and industry sponsors interested in pursuing the development of individualized gene editing therapies under the plausible mechanism framework (while also containing much of the technical information supporting the primary data presented in this perspective), we have made our Pre-IND briefing book and the FDA’s written responses available on the SCGE Translational Coordination and Dissemination Center website: https://scge.mcw.edu/platform/public/documents/regulatory.
